subsection: 4. The outbreak of the Troubles: from 1969 to Direct Rule, 1972

notes.h: Background to 1969: Stormont, grievances and the security forces
notes.b: By 1969 Northern Ireland had been governed for almost fifty years by one party, and many Catholics felt shut out of the state. Knowing what had built up before August 1969 explains why the violence broke out so quickly once it started.
points: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 set up the Northern Ireland parliament (Stormont), and the Unionist Party governed from 1921 to 1972. Westminster kept sovereignty but in practice rarely interfered in Northern Ireland's internal affairs.

The Ireland Act 1949 guaranteed that Northern Ireland would stay in the United Kingdom unless its parliament (later its people) consented, which is why unionists treated any talk of change as a threat to the border.
Catholics complained of discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting. The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA), founded in 1967, campaigned on these grievances through marches.

A NICRA march in Derry on 5 October 1968 and the attack on a People's Democracy march at Burntollet in January 1969 deepened tension, and the Prime Minister, Terence O'Neill, resigned on 28 April 1969. Such marches mattered because they brought the grievances onto the streets.

The RUC (Royal Ulster Constabulary) was the regular police, armed and mostly Protestant. The B Specials (the Ulster Special Constabulary) were a part-time reserve, almost entirely Protestant, and Catholics distrusted both.
The IRA's border campaign of 1956-62 had failed, and Stormont had used internment (detention without trial) against it in the 1950s, so the IRA was weak and divided in 1969.
notes.tip: Examiners expect long-term causes (discrimination, policing) to be separated from the triggers of 1969-72. Combine the long-term causes with the triggers and the factors that sustained the conflict.

notes.h: Key concepts: terrorism, sectarianism, internment and Direct Rule
notes.b: Four terms run through this period, and each is used in a specific way in this topic. Defining them first makes the events easier to follow.
points: Terrorism means violence against civilians and the state for political aims. In this topic it applies to both republican and loyalist paramilitaries, and examiners reward answers that name both sides.

Sectarianism means hostility between Protestants and Catholics based on religious identity and political allegiance, so an attack on a Catholic or Protestant as such, not as a soldier or politician, is sectarian.
Internment means detaining suspects without trial, so people could be held on suspicion alone. It was introduced in August 1971 and applied almost entirely to Catholics.
Direct Rule means that Northern Ireland was governed directly from Westminster, through a Secretary of State, instead of by the Stormont parliament. It began on 30 March 1972.

notes.h: August 1969: Derry and Belfast erupt, and the police reforms that followed
notes.b: The Apprentice Boys' parade in Derry in August 1969 led to street fighting, and British troops were sent in to restore order. The crisis then forced London to take a hand in policing and reform.
points: On 12 August 1969 the parade of the Apprentice Boys of Derry passed close to the Bogside (a Catholic area of Derry), and stone-throwing and clashes with the RUC began.
The Battle of the Bogside lasted from 12 to 14 August 1969. Residents put up barricades, which created the 'Free Derry' area.

British troops were deployed in Derry on 14 August 1969 and in Belfast shortly afterwards, on 15 August. This was the start of the army's long involvement in internal security. The UK Prime Minister was Harold Wilson (Labour).
Rioting in Belfast on 14 and 15 August 1969 saw Catholic streets such as Bombay Street in the Lower Falls burned and several people killed, most of them Catholics.

Thousands of families, most of them Catholic, fled their homes in Belfast, and refugee centres were set up in the Republic and in Catholic parishes. August 1969 is also often treated as the start of the Troubles in their most violent form.

The Downing Street Declaration of 19 August 1969, issued by Wilson and Chichester-Clark, restated that Northern Ireland would not cease to be part of the United Kingdom without the consent of its people, and promised reforms.

The Hunt Report, published on 10 October 1969 by a committee led by Lord Hunt, recommended a reformed, unarmed RUC under a police authority, so that the police would no longer look like a partisan armed force. It also said the B Specials should be replaced.

The B Specials (Ulster Special Constabulary) were stood down in April 1970. The Ulster Defence Regiment, a part-time regiment of the British army formed in 1970, took over their local security duties.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the 1969 Downing Street Declaration (Wilson, the consent guarantee and reform) with the 1993 declaration of the peace process. Add the date to avoid the confusion.

notes.b: Chichester-Clark's two years as Prime Minister saw reform under pressure from London and a rising tide of violence. He could satisfy neither unionist hardliners nor nationalists.
points: James Chichester-Clark became Prime Minister on 1 May 1969, defeating Brian Faulkner in the party vote by 17 votes to 16, a very narrow margin that left Faulkner as his rival.
He presided over the Battle of the Bogside and the disbanding of the B Specials, and London pressed him to carry out the reforms of the Hunt Report.

His government announced a points system for housing allocation, which made the awarding of council houses fairer, the creation of a Housing Executive (established in 1971) and reform of local government.
Unionist hardliners saw these steps as surrender, while nationalists said they came too late, so the reforms won him little credit from either side.
He resigned on 20 March 1971 after London would not give him the security measures he wanted.
Brian Faulkner succeeded him as Prime Minister on 23 March 1971, so the man he had narrowly beaten in 1969 took over because security policy had failed.
notes.tip: Keep the three Prime Ministers straight: O'Neill (to April 1969), Chichester-Clark (1969-71) and Faulkner (1971-72).

notes.h: The Provisional IRA, the SDLP and Alliance, 1969-1970
notes.b: August 1969 convinced many Catholics that the IRA had failed to protect them, and the movement split. At the same time new political parties appeared, offering constitutional alternatives to violence.
points: The IRA split in December 1969 into the Provisional IRA, whose chief of staff was Seán Mac Stíofáin, and the Official IRA, led by Cathal Goulding.

The split followed the failure to defend Catholic areas in August 1969, which discredited the old leadership, and a dispute over abstentionism (refusing to take seats in parliaments) and the political, socialist direction.
The Provisionals argued that the IRA must defend Catholic areas and that British forces should be driven out, in pursuit of a united Ireland. This position gained support after August 1969.
Provisional Sinn Féin was set up in January 1970 to match the new military wing, so the Provisionals had a political party as well as an army.
The Falls curfew of 3 to 5 July 1970 saw troops search houses for weapons in the Lower Falls, and four civilians were killed. The operation alienated Catholics from the army.
The Alliance Party was founded in April 1970 as a cross-community party, and it later chose Oliver Napier as leader.

The Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) was founded on 21 August 1970 by nationalist politicians including Gerry Fitt (leader), John Hume, Austin Currie and Paddy Devlin. It stood for constitutional nationalism, seeking change by political means.
The SDLP withdrew from Stormont in July 1971 after the army shot dead two men in Derry, Séamus Cusack and Desmond Beattie.
The Official IRA, which stressed a left-wing political strategy, declared a ceasefire in May 1972, which left the Provisionals as the main republican force.
notes.tip: For a short answer on the IRA split, give the date (December 1969), the two groups with their leaders, and the Provisionals' aims. Do not confuse Provisional Sinn Féin with the Official party.

notes.b: Loyalist paramilitary groups grew in response to the republican campaign and to the fear that the Union was under threat. They attacked Catholic civilians and republicans, which fed the cycle of reprisal.
points: The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) was revived in 1966 and killed three people that year. In the early years of the Troubles it carried out attacks on Catholic targets. It was a small, secretive killer group.

The Ulster Defence Association (UDA), a loose umbrella of loyalist vigilante groups, was formed in 1971 and grew rapidly in working-class Protestant areas. It was a legal organisation until 1992, which marks it out from the UVF.
The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 Catholic civilians. The police first blamed the IRA, but the Police Ombudsman's report of 2011 found that the UVF was responsible.
Loyalist groups claimed that their violence defended the Union and Protestant areas, but most of their victims were Catholic civilians, which is why their violence is called sectarian.
William Craig founded the Ulster Vanguard movement in 1972, which held large rallies against the loss of Stormont's powers.
notes.tip: Examiners reward naming both republican and loyalist terrorism. Remember the contrast: the UVF was a small killer group, the UDA a mass umbrella that was legal until 1992.

notes.h: Key personality: Brian Faulkner (part 1, as Prime Minister)
notes.b: Faulkner was the Prime Minister who introduced internment and then saw his government collapse under the pressure of violence and British policy. His career is followed here only up to March 1972.
points: Brian Faulkner, born in 1921, was a Unionist businessman and politician. He was Minister of Home Affairs in 1959-63 and Minister of Commerce in 1963-69, and he resigned from O'Neill's cabinet in 1969.
He lost the party vote to Chichester-Clark by 17 to 16 in 1969, but became Prime Minister on 23 March 1971, winning the party vote against William Craig.
He asked London to authorise internment, which began on 9 August 1971 under the UK Prime Minister, Edward Heath. Faulkner defended it as necessary to stop the IRA, but it hardened Catholic opinion.

In June 1971 he offered the opposition committee chairmanships at Stormont. The SDLP did not take up the offer and withdrew from Stormont in July 1971 after the Derry shootings, so his attempt to draw nationalists in failed.

He talked with Heath about control of security and insisted that Stormont should keep its powers over policing and order. He and his ministers resigned on 24 March 1972 because he refused London's demand to transfer security powers.
He was shaped by events: the violence, the SDLP withdrawal, Bloody Sunday and London's demand for security powers ended his government.
Contemporary unionists praised his firmness on security, while nationalists saw internment as a deliberate attack on the Catholic community.

He was a participant who wrote of events from the inside in his memoirs, published in 1978 after his death in 1977. Historians generally see him as a pragmatic, able, reforming politician whose attempts at reform were swamped by violence he could not contain.
notes.tip: Higher questions ask for strengths and weaknesses or his contribution, so use paired success and failure points, each with a date and a result. For Ordinary Level, give who he was, the offices he held, how he became Prime Minister, what he did, why it failed and how it ended.

notes.h: Internment and the Ballymurphy killings, August 1971
notes.b: Internment was introduced on 9 August 1971 to break the IRA, but it was applied almost entirely to republicans, and the violence that followed killed civilians.
points: Internment, the detention of suspects without trial, began on 9 August 1971 in Operation Demetrius, which arrested about 340 people in its first sweep. The intelligence used was poor, so many of those arrested had no paramilitary links.
Those arrested were almost entirely Catholic, and no loyalist was interned until 1973. This is why nationalists saw internment as proof of bias.
Interrogation methods known as the five techniques, which included hooding and sleep deprivation, were used on fourteen internees, known as the Hooded Men.
The Compton and Parker inquiries examined the methods, and in 1978 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the techniques were inhuman and degrading treatment, but not torture.

At Ballymurphy in west Belfast, eleven civilians died during army operations of 9 to 11 August 1971, including a priest, Father Hugh Mullan. A coroner's inquest in 2021 found that those killed were innocent.
Internment increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA. Separately, 1971 was the first year in which Troubles deaths passed 100.
notes.tip: Do not mix up internment (August 1971), the Ballymurphy killings (the same days in August 1971) and the Falls curfew (July 1970). For Ordinary Level, remember when and who introduced internment, and what Faulkner asked London for.

notes.b: A civil rights march in Derry against internment ended with British paratroopers killing thirteen civilians, an event that deepened the conflict. Many nationalists lost confidence in the army and the state.
points: The NICRA march of 30 January 1972 in Derry protested against internment and was banned by the authorities.

Soldiers of the 1st Battalion, Parachute Regiment, entered the Bogside and fired on marchers and bystanders, killing thirteen people on the day, so a banned but peaceful protest became a massacre in nationalist eyes.
A fourteenth man who was wounded died some months later, and most of the dead were shot while unarmed or while fleeing.
The Widgery Report of 19 April 1972, by the Lord Chief Justice, largely accepted the army's account, and nationalists widely rejected it as a whitewash.
The Saville Inquiry, reporting on 15 June 2010, found that soldiers of 1 PARA caused the deaths and injuries and that no casualty had posed a threat of causing death or serious injury.
In his statement to the Commons that day, the Prime Minister, David Cameron, called the killings 'unjustified and unjustifiable' and apologised.

The killings led to the burning of the British embassy in Dublin on 2 February 1972, and they increased recruitment to the Provisional IRA, because nationalist confidence in the army and the state broke down.
notes.tip: A common weakness is confusing Bloody Sunday (30 January 1972, Derry, paratroopers, thirteen killed) with Bloody Friday (21 July 1972, Belfast, IRA bombs, nine killed). Give a one-line identification with date and place. Attribute the words 'unjustified and unjustifiable' to Cameron, not to Saville.

notes.h: Stormont suspended and Direct Rule, March 1972
notes.b: Stormont was suspended and government was taken over by Westminster after Faulkner's government refused to hand security powers to London. This was the end of the Unionist government that had ruled since 1921.
points: London, under Edward Heath, demanded that control of security be transferred to Westminster. Faulkner's government refused.
Faulkner and his ministers resigned on 24 March 1972 in protest, and Westminster suspended the Stormont parliament from 30 March.
The Northern Ireland (Temporary Provisions) Act 1972 introduced Direct Rule from 30 March 1972, placing the province under a Secretary of State.

William Whitelaw was the first Secretary of State for Northern Ireland and governed with civil servants, two ministers of state and the army. The Stormont parliament was formally abolished in 1973 by the Northern Ireland Constitution Act.
Whitelaw granted special category status to paramilitary prisoners in June 1972. He met leaders of the Provisional IRA in London on 7 July 1972 during a short ceasefire, but the talks failed.
Unionists reacted with anger because they felt abandoned, and Craig's Vanguard held large rallies against the loss of Stormont's powers, while nationalists welcomed the end of Stormont.

Direct Rule was meant to be temporary, but apart from the executive of 1 January to 28 May 1974 it continued until the 1990s, because the parties could not agree a power-sharing settlement acceptable to both communities.

Direct Rule lasted because unionists would not accept an assembly with nationalist participation, nationalists would not accept a return to majority rule, and London wished to avoid a return to the old system.
notes.tip: Get the direction right: London demanded security powers, Faulkner refused, and Stormont fell. Do not say Faulkner demanded them. Stormont was suspended on 30 March 1972 but only abolished in 1973. Essays need a causal argument (loss of control of security, internment, Bloody Sunday) and then why Direct Rule lasted.

notes.h: Bloody Friday and Operation Motorman, July 1972
notes.b: The IRA bombings of 21 July 1972 killed nine people in Belfast, and ten days later the army's Operation Motorman broke the IRA's no-go areas. Violence in 1972 reached its peak.
points: On 21 July 1972, the Provisional IRA set off about twenty bombs in Belfast in the space of about an hour and a half, a day that became known as Bloody Friday.
Nine people died in the bombings and about 130 were injured, and the attacks shocked public opinion in Britain and Northern Ireland.

Operation Motorman, launched on 31 July 1972 with about 12,000 soldiers, moved into the no-go areas (districts the army and police could not enter) in Belfast and Derry, including the Creggan and the Bogside.
The operation cleared the barricades and restored government control, so areas that the IRA had controlled came back under the state.
The IRA's campaign continued after Motorman, which is why 1972 was the deadliest year of the Troubles, with nearly 500 deaths.
notes.tip: Operation Motorman (31 July 1972) was the army operation; do not confuse it with the Claudy bombing of the same day, a car-bomb attack in a village in which nine were killed. Keep Bloody Friday (Belfast, IRA bombs, nine dead) apart from Bloody Sunday.

notes.h: Why the Troubles erupted and lasted
notes.b: The Troubles had long-term causes, short-term triggers and factors that kept them going. A good answer separates these and judges which mattered most.
points: Discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting gave the civil rights movement a sustained base of grievance, and unionist fear of change made reform hard.
The state's security forces, the B Specials and the RUC, were seen by Catholics as partisan, which turned protest into a security issue.
British misjudgement also played a part, because London had long left Northern Ireland's affairs alone and it misjudged the situation.
The Provisional IRA gave the Catholic community a military organisation, and its campaign drew the British army into the conflict.
Loyalist paramilitaries defended Protestant areas and attacked Catholic civilians, which increased the cycle of reprisal.
The army and internment alienated Catholics, and internment and Bloody Sunday hardened attitudes on both sides and made political compromise harder.
Stormont's inability to share power with nationalists meant there was no political institution capable of containing the violence.
The decline of Stormont had many causes: civil rights protest, the failure to reform fast enough, the IRA campaign, and the British government's decision to take over security.
notes.tip: For the Higher essay, combine long-term causes (discrimination, policing) with triggers (August 1969, the IRA split, internment, Bloody Sunday) and sustaining factors (paramilitaries, no political institution), and give a clear judgement on the most important cause.

notes.h: Assessment: Direct Rule and the failure of Stormont
notes.b: Direct Rule can be judged as an achievement or a failure, and contemporaries judged it differently from later historians. Examiners reward paired points on both sides.
points: Achievement: the end of Stormont removed an institution that nationalists had rejected since 1921, and it opened the way for later settlements.
Failure: the Stormont government could not contain the violence, and its reliance on internment alienated the Catholic community.
Contemporary view: unionists saw the suspension of Stormont as a betrayal by Westminster, while nationalists welcomed it as the end of an unfair system, and were relieved.
Contemporary view: the British government saw Direct Rule as a temporary arrangement, but it proved to be a long-term one.
Later view: historians argue that the 1972 settlement was forced by violence, and that the Unionist government's decline was a product of its own policies as well as republican action.
notes.tip: Name both sides: unionist and nationalist views of internment and Direct Rule. A narrative of 1971-72 without cause and judgement scores poorly.
